**Published online:**
September 2, 2026 (Reuters, Providence, Rhode Island dateline)

**Geographic focus:**
United States (primary); Global (secondary — reference to overseas central banks, global governments, Iran energy price risk)

**Temporal focus:**
T1. Historical report [YES] — documents structural shifts in Treasury market over past two decades
T2. Forward-looking reporting short-term risks (next few weeks/months) [YES] — near-term inflation uncertainty, Iran/energy risk, ongoing supply/demand imbalance
T3. Forward-looking reporting long-term risks (next quarters/years) [YES] — structural deficit trajectory, AI capex borrowing wave, term premium repricing, buyer base shift

**Synopsis:**
Long-end US Treasury yields face persistent upward pressure from a confluence of structural and cyclical forces. Supply is surging — both from the federal government (debt >$40T, widening deficits) and investment-grade corporates (AI infrastructure buildout driving $730B+ capex spend in 2026). Simultaneously, demand is deteriorating as price-insensitive buyers (foreign central banks) have been replaced by price-sensitive ones (hedge funds), increasing market volatility and yield sensitivity. Term premium is rising, inflation remains above the Fed's 2% target, and geopolitical risk (Iran/energy) adds further uncertainty. Treasury Secretary Bessent's efforts to suppress long-term borrowing costs are seen by bond market participants as structurally constrained — both supply and demand dynamics are largely outside policy control.
